details:
Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

WHAT IT DOES

OUTPOST: Survive the Sol is a browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon outpost (Shackleton rim) or a Mars outpost (Jezero Crater) for 30 sols. Every sol, players read a forecast of the next event (a solar storm, dust storm, equipment fault, or comms blackout), then share one limited power budget between four jobs: life support, a radiation shield, a greenhouse, and science. Three meters (power, air, and shielding) keep the screen simple.

No choice is free. Shielding costs power that the plants need, skimping on air hurts crew health, and the Moon's long night (sols 16 to 30) cuts solar power, so energy has to be stored in the battery by day. On Mars, advice from Earth arrives 3 to 22 minutes late, so the crew decides alone. If a mission fails, the mission replay shows the exact sol and trade-off that went wrong, and every mission has its own code so players can try again and improve.

HOW NASA DATA IS USED

- NASA DONKI (space weather): recent solar flare and CME records appear in a "Real NASA Space Weather" panel. In Today's Real Space Weather mode, the strongest event sets the storm baseline: an M-class flare is level 2 and an X-class flare is level 3.

- NASA OSDR RadLab: a real ISS absorbed dose rate (5.9 microgray per hour, from 1 to 2 April 2022) calibrates how fast crew radiation dose builds up.

- NASA OSDR study search: each mission ends with a real NASA space-biology study.

- CSA food-production toolkit: greenhouse facts, rewritten in kid-friendly words.

Every NASA card is labeled LIVE or with the date of its snapshot. The game fetches from NASA when the browser can reach it and falls back to a dated snapshot (fetched 14 Nov 2026) otherwise. Nothing static is shown as live, and cards without verified data are hidden.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids feel why mission planners must balance power, air, and safety, and why a crew far from Earth has to decide for itself. The game runs in any browser with no download or account. It includes a three-step tutorial and a classroom mode with discussion questions for teachers and parents.

HOW IT IS BUILT

Vite, TypeScript, and an animated SVG outpost scene. The simulation engine is separate from the interface and is tested with Vitest. Playwright runs full missions on desktop and phone-sized screens, and axe-core checks accessibility. Automated simulations of 500 missions per strategy keep the difficulty fair: random or do-nothing play loses, and reading the forecast and planning ahead wins. Hosted on Vercel.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a quiz or a poster, the trade-off is the game. A forecast before each sol turns real mission planning into a decision, and the replay turns failure into a lesson.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Only three meters, so a 7-year-old can follow. Plain language, with science terms explained in context. No free choices. Honest labeling of data sources.

AI ASSISTANCE

Code and planning were assisted by AI tools (Codex, Antigravity, Claude). The concept, design choices, and learning goals are the team's own.
